title: The Uncapped Ledger
subtitle: How Malaysia's Real Fiscal Exposure Hides Outside the Number Everyone Argues About
stageScoresNote: Reviewed across multiple stages, including a second fact-verification pass on the corrected text. The first review flagged several errors, all since corrected: a wrong claim that total federal debt is uncapped, a conflation of total and committed guarantees, a misread fuel-subsidy figure, an overstated stress-test description, and a wrong working-age-to-retiree ratio. The re-review confirmed the corrections (factual-accuracy 86) and the dossier as fit for publication, with the remaining framing edits since applied. Figures are dated end-June 2025 (MOF Fiscal Outlook 2026); the forward debt-path and pension figures are labelled illustrations and projections, not observed facts.
finalScoreNote: Every reader-facing actual is verified against a primary source (MOF Fiscal Outlook 2026, IMF Article IV 2026, Act 850, DOSM): statutory debt 63.5%, total federal debt 64.7%, all-in 84.1%, the 2024 deficit of 4.1%, guarantees RM424.7 billion, retirement charges, and the demographic dependency path. The debt-path and pension trajectories are labelled illustrations and projections on stated assumptions, not observed facts.

sections.title: The Uncapped Ledger
sections.subtitle: How Malaysia's real fiscal exposure hides outside the number everyone argues about
whatYoullLearn: Why Malaysia has three different debt numbers, and which one the law actually caps
How the country beat its deficit target while still missing its own Fiscal Responsibility Act
Where the RM424.7 billion in guarantees and the rising pension bill sit on the books
Two debt paths to 2035, and the assumptions that decide which one happens

sections.title: The dossier in 7 lines
bullets: Malaysia reports three nested debt figures: statutory debt 63.5%, total federal debt 64.7%, and total debt plus liabilities 84.1% of GDP (end-June 2025).
Only statutory debt is bound by the hard 65% ceiling. Total federal debt has a softer 60% medium-term benchmark, and the all-in 84.1% figure has no aggregate statutory cap at all.
The 2024 deficit came in at 4.1%, beating the annual target, yet the Fiscal Responsibility Act benchmarks of 3% deficit and 60% debt are both still being missed.

Total financial guarantees stand at RM424.7 billion (21.1% of GDP), of which about RM237 billion is committed. Under the Finance Ministry's own contingent-liability stress test, debt could peak near 97% of GDP.
Civil-service retirement charges reach RM42.8 billion in 2026 and are projected toward RM120 billion by 2040, none of it counted against the debt ceiling.
The working-age base behind each retiree is set to roughly halve by 2040 as the old-age dependency ratio doubles.
The fiscal debate fixates on one reassuring figure. The exposure that matters sits about twenty points higher.

sections.title: The Numbers Behind the Number
sections.subtitle: Why 64% and 84% are both true at the same time

sections.title: Three debt numbers, one ceiling
sections.body:
Ask how indebted Malaysia is and you can get three honest answers. Statutory debt, the measure of Malaysian Government Securities, Government Investment Issues and Treasury bills, stood at 63.5% of GDP at end-June 2025. Total federal government debt, which adds other instruments, was 64.7%. Total debt and liabilities, which adds committed guarantees and other obligations, reached 84.1%, about RM1.69 trillion.

The distinction is not pedantry. The hard 65% ceiling written into law in 2021 binds only the first measure. The second carries a softer 60% medium-term benchmark under the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act, and the all-in 84.1% figure sits under no aggregate statutory cap at all. So when coverage reports that debt is 64% and still under the ceiling, the number being reassured about is not the number the ceiling governs.

sections.title: Beat the target, missed the law
sections.body:
The 2024 fiscal deficit came in at 4.1% of GDP, inside the 4.3% target the government had set for the year. That was reported, fairly, as a win. The targets for 2025 and 2026 are 3.8% and 3.5%.

The quieter fact: the Public Finance and Fiscal Responsibility Act 2023 sets a medium-term benchmark of a deficit no greater than 3% and debt no greater than 60% of GDP. Both are still being missed. The IMF, in its 2026 Article IV review, endorsed the consolidation path, with its baseline reaching 3% only in 2028 and federal debt still around 61% of GDP in 2030, above the 60% target. Beating a discretionary annual target and meeting a statutory benchmark are different achievements, and only one of them has happened.
citations: MOF, Malaysia Exceeds GDP and Fiscal Deficit Targets for 2024
MOF Fiscal Outlook 2026, fiscal balance section
IMF Article IV Consultation 2026, Executive Board conclusion
Public Finance and Fiscal Responsibility Act 2023 (Act 850)

sections.body: The headline is not wrong. It is the wrong number. The figure that is legally capped, statutory debt, is the one chosen to look reassuring. The figure that captures real exposure, the all-in 84.1%, is the one no ceiling touches.

sections.title: The Fork
sections.subtitle: Where the trajectory splits, and what bends it

sections.title: Two paths from 64.7%
sections.body:
Debt dynamics are governed by a simple recursion: this year's debt ratio equals last year's, scaled by interest and growth, plus the primary deficit. With an effective interest rate near 4.1% on the domestic stock, two assumptions decide everything: how fast nominal GDP grows, and whether the primary deficit keeps shrinking.

The two lines below are a T4A illustration of total federal debt, not an official forecast. Hold to a consolidation glide-path, with nominal growth near 6% and the primary deficit falling toward balance, and the ratio drifts down toward the high 50s by 2035, close to where the Finance Ministry's own baseline points it by 2030. Let growth slip to 4.5% and the primary deficit stick near 1.1%, and the same start climbs into the low 70s. The Finance Ministry and the IMF publish their own scenarios to 2030 and 2031; ours simply shows how far apart two plausible paths sit. The gap is not luck. It is policy.

sections.title: What bends the path
sections.body: Three levers move the trajectory. The first is the subsidy bill: the RON95 rationalisation launched in September 2025, paired with the BUDI95 targeted subsidy programme that holds most motorists at RM1.99 a litre, was projected to save around RM2.5 to RM4 billion a year, down from earlier talk of RM8 billion. Those savings stay oil-price sensitive: the subsidy cost falls when global crude eases, as it did in late 2025, and would climb again if crude rises. The second is debt service, already about 16% of revenue in 2025 and near 17% in 2026. The third is growth itself, the denominator that flatters or punishes every ratio. None of the three is locked in, which is precisely why the fork stays open.
citations: MOF Fiscal Updates 2025, BUDI95 rollout and debt service
Reuters, Malaysia cuts savings estimate from fuel subsidy change (23 Sept 2025)
MOF Fiscal Outlook 2026, expenditure and debt service sections

sections.title: The Liabilities With No Ceiling
sections.subtitle: Guarantees, pensions, and the support base behind them

sections.title: Four hundred billion in guarantees
sections.body: Beyond the debt sits RM424.7 billion in total financial guarantees, about 21.1% of GDP, below the 25% cap that Act 850 places on them. Of that, roughly RM237 billion is counted as committed in the all-in liabilities table, alongside about RM153 billion in other obligations including public-private partnerships. The largest guarantee exposures sit with infrastructure and financing vehicles such as DanaInfra Nasional and the public-sector housing and student-loan funds. The Finance Ministry's own stress test is blunt: model a contingent-liability shock worth 15% of GDP and debt peaks near 97% of GDP in 2027. These are contingent, not certain. But they are real, and they move with infrastructure and financing decisions that rarely reach the fiscal headlines.
citations: MOF Fiscal Outlook 2026, Section 5 Fiscal Risk and Liabilities
MOF Fiscal Outlook 2026, Section 4 debt sustainability analysis (contingent-liability shock)
The Star, combined debt and liabilities touch 84.1% of GDP

sections.title: The pension bill that answers to no ceiling
sections.body:
Civil-service retirement charges are climbing fast: the Finance Ministry's own figures put them at RM35.9 billion in 2024, RM40.1 billion in 2025 and RM42.8 billion in 2026, with the number of pensioners heading toward one million. The government's own projection, reported in Parliament, has the bill reaching about RM46 billion by 2030 and RM120 billion by 2040.

Emoluments and retirement charges together already absorb about 45% of operating expenditure in the 2026 estimate. And the promise is mostly pay-as-you-go: a dedicated fund, KWAP, covers only a slice (its contribution is set near RM5 billion against RM42.8 billion of charges in 2026), so the bulk is paid from current revenue, sits off the debt-to-GDP ratio, and falls under no statutory cap.
citations: MOF Fiscal Outlook 2026, Section 3 Expenditure (retirement charges 2024 to 2026)
New Straits Times, government pension payout, citing Dewan Rakyat answer (13 Mar 2024)
The Star, government spent RM116.7bil on pensions 2020 to 2023 (14 Mar 2024)

sections.title: Fewer shoulders under each retiree
sections.body: The pension promise is paid largely as you go, out of current revenue, so the base of working-age taxpayers matters as much as the bill itself. Today around nine working-age adults stand behind each Malaysian aged 65 and over. On the official projection, the old-age dependency ratio roughly doubles by 2040, reaching about 21.7 per hundred, which leaves fewer than five working-age adults behind each retiree. A rising obligation, met by a shrinking base, is the part of the pension story the annual figures never show.

sections.title: Why none of it is capped
sections.body: The discipline in law is split. A 65% ceiling on statutory debt comes from the borrowing statutes; the Fiscal Responsibility Act adds quantified medium-term values for the deficit, the debt level, and financial guarantees, and requires an adjustment plan when they are missed. But the Act sets no aggregate ceiling on total debt plus liabilities, none on the pension obligation, and none on the shrinking support base that funds the pension promise. The result is a ledger where the most disciplined number is also the least complete, and the largest exposures grow in the space the law reports but does not cap. This is not hidden in the sense of concealed. It is published, in tables one page away from the figure that gets quoted.

sections.claim: Malaysia's debt is 64% of GDP and safely under the 65% ceiling, so the fiscal position is sound.
sections.correction: 64.7% is total federal debt; the hard 65% ceiling binds only the narrower statutory measure at 63.5%, while total federal debt carries a softer 60% medium-term benchmark it already exceeds. Add committed guarantees and other liabilities and the all-in figure is 84.1%, with a stress case near 97%. The ceiling governs the narrowest of three numbers.

sections.source: Public Finance and Fiscal Responsibility Act 2023 (Act 850), First Schedule (paraphrased)
sections.body: The Act's medium-term values put the deficit at no more than 3% of GDP and federal debt at no more than 60%.
sections.commentary: Both values are set in statute as medium-term objectives. Both are currently exceeded, with the government's and the IMF's own paths reaching the 3% deficit only in 2028.

sections.title: How the ceiling moved
sections.intro: The statutory debt ceiling is not a constant. It has been raised twice in five years, each time to accommodate the borrowing of the moment.

sections.body: A ceiling that rises to meet the debt is not a constraint on the debt. It is a record of it.

sections.title: What to watch, in order
sections.body: Four signals tell you which path Malaysia is on, well before the annual budget does. Watch debt service as a share of revenue: once it passes a sixth of every ringgit collected, the room to consolidate narrows. Watch the realised subsidy savings against the early talk of RM8 billion. Watch nominal growth, the denominator that does the quiet work. And watch whether the next budget caps anything beyond statutory debt. The headline ratio will be the last thing to move, not the first.

Malaysia's fiscal managers are not reckless, and the consolidation since 2023 is real. The danger is narrative, not arithmetic: a debate anchored on the one number the law happens to cap, while the exposures that carry no ceiling, guarantees, pensions, and a thinning tax base, compound out of view. A government can beat a target it sets itself. It cannot, for long, outgrow the obligations it does not count.
